A reinvestment rule can leave cash behind: whole shares, fractions and the full account value

Follow distributions through whole-share and fractional purchases in four charts, keeping residual cash beside the security value and testing both positive and negative return assumptions.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Trace whole-share purchases, fractional purchases and retained distribution cash

Interactive planning lab

Whole-share rule: final security value plus cash$6,347.82
Whole-share rule: final unspent distribution cash$40.9
Final resources: fractional rule less whole-share rule$33.58

Original hypothetical comparison of two purchase rules for one fictional distribution-paying security. Both start with the same whole shares and no cash, add no outside money and consume nothing. Four equal periods per year share the same assumed total-return factor. Each period’s price first grows by that factor, then a fixed distribution per share is deducted: starting price × entered annual distribution percentage ÷ 4. This is a constructed valuation path, not an actual ex-dividend price prediction. Distributions depend on shares owned before that period’s purchase. Both rules pool old residual cash with the new distribution and purchase at the same post-distribution price. One buys the maximum whole shares; the other allows unlimited fractional precision. Remaining cash earns zero. Pooling old residual cash is an explicit purchase rule and may differ from a broker’s automatic plan. There are no fees, taxes, spreads, discounts, settlement delays, rounding to a broker’s precision, contribution-room calculations or guaranteed payments. All figures are nominal CAD. Fractional reinvestment maintains more exposure to the assumed security path; it does not ensure a better outcome in every return scenario.

The central idea

Buying more shares changes where resources are held. Compare the complete account, including cash, before interpreting the effect of a reinvestment instruction.

01

Define the purchase rule before assuming every distribution is invested

A distribution can be too small to buy one additional share. A rule limited to whole shares may leave cash behind, while a fractional purchase can put more of that cash into the security. The amount actually invested depends on the plan’s terms and execution.

The SEC’s fractional-share bulletin explains that availability, execution and fees vary by brokerage. Fractional ownership generally participates in dividends in proportion to the fraction owned. An account’s available securities and precision still need checking.

This tool compares two invented purchase rules. Both pool old residual cash with each new quarterly distribution. One buys as many whole shares as possible; the other permits unlimited fractional precision. A real automatic reinvestment plan may not use old cash this way, so the model should not be read as a description of every DRIP.

02

Give both holders the same starting investment and price path

The default account begins with 20 shares at CAD 250, worth CAD 5,000, and no cash. There are no later contributions or withdrawals. Each of the four equal periods per year has the same factor derived from an assumed 5% annual total return.

The quarterly distribution is fixed at 1% of the starting price: CAD 2.50 per share. In the constructed valuation path, the price first grows by the quarterly total-return factor and then falls by that per-share distribution. Both holders trade at the same resulting price.

This price rule is an accounting illustration, not a forecast of an actual security around an ex-dividend date. A 4% scheduled distribution and a 5% total-return assumption are different inputs; adding them together would count the distribution twice. The model excludes taxes, trading costs, spreads and actual execution delays.

03

Reconcile the first distribution without creating an extra gain

In the first quarter, the original 20 shares generate CAD 50 of cash. The modeled post-distribution price is about CAD 250.5681. The whole-share rule cannot buy a share, so it retains 20 shares worth about CAD 5,011.36 and CAD 50 in cash.

The fractional rule uses that CAD 50 to buy about 0.1995 additional shares. Its security value is about CAD 5,061.36 and its cash is zero. The whole-share account’s security plus cash is also CAD 5,061.36.

The purchase has moved resources from cash to shares. It has not created an immediate gain. The first stacked bars make that equality visible before later exposure to returns produces a difference.

04

Carry the remainder into the next purchase rather than discarding it

Under the whole-share rule, each new distribution joins the cash left from earlier periods. The rule buys a share when that combined pool is large enough. A drop in the cash line can therefore represent a purchase rather than spending or an investment loss.

After each purchase, residual cash is smaller than the cost of one share at that period’s price. The cash remains part of account value. Ignoring it would understate the resources held by the whole-share account.

Additional shares participate in distributions only from the following modeled period. The amount paid therefore depends on the shares owned before that quarter’s reinvestment. The price path itself remains common to both holders.

05

Separate reinvestment exposure from a promise of better performance

After five default years, the whole-share rule owns 24 shares plus about CAD 40.90 in cash. At the common price of about CAD 262.7886, its total resources are about CAD 6,347.82.

The unlimited-fraction rule owns about 24.2834 shares and no material cash, worth about CAD 6,381.41. This matches CAD 5,000 compounded at the assumed 5% total return for five years. Its advantage is about CAD 33.58 in this particular path.

The difference arises because cash earning zero has less exposure to the assumed positive security return. When the assumed security return is negative, keeping some cash can instead cushion losses. With zero total return and no costs, both rules preserve starting resources in this constructed path, even while distributions and share counts change.

The matrix expresses the final resource difference as a percentage of each scenario’s starting investment. It varies starting share count and total return. It does not report an annualised return, a probability or evidence that a larger distribution guarantees better results.

06

Check the actual account instruction and the role of its cash

The Investor.gov explanation of direct investment and dividend reinvestment plans recommends reviewing disclosure documents and possible charges. For an actual account, check eligible securities, purchase precision, residual-cash handling, execution timing and fees.

Then decide how much cash belongs in the account for upcoming expenses or other commitments. A household that needs the distribution for a bill has a different objective from this illustration, which retains every dollar and consumes nothing.

Reinvestment changes exposure, transaction records and the mix of security value and cash. It does not establish suitability, create new contribution room or remove any applicable tax obligation. Those questions require the actual account, investment and tax context.
